body_markdown:
## Key Takeaways for Investors


-


Bitcoin decouples from the yield spike. As the ten year bond (10Y) yields hit levels not seen since 2007, bitcoin is trading as a hedge against the fiat system rather than an S&P 500 beta play.


-


Agencies keep building while the IRS targets tax strategies. The IRS shut down 351 conversions, which don't implicate spot crypto ETFs, but other tax-advantaged strategies are on notice.


-


**Schrödinger's Wallet:** The $352M Bitget exploit shows exchanges are still crypto's weakest link, and those insecurities directly affect geopolitical stability.


## Bond Market Calls Treasury's Bluff. Bitcoin Isn't Flinching.


On Aug 19, the U.S. Treasury Department announced it would at least double the maximum size of its liquidity support buybacks on the long end, from $2 billion to at least $4 billion, effective Sep 9. Markets initially responded as one would expect. The 10Y slipped, while bitcoin and gold rallied. The relief did not last, however. By the time a triple-the-normal-level buyback took effect on September 9th, up to $6B, the 10Y had climbed precipitously, casting doubt on Treasury’s ability to control interest rates.


Today, things look even bleaker, with the 10Y hitting 5.27%, a level it hasn’t hit since 2007. It reads like a referendum on the Treasury's inability to contain rates, with bond vigilantes calling Bessent’s bluff. Note: it is highly unusual for the Treasury to intervene in its own borrowing costs, that’s usually the job of the Fed, but here Chair Warsh isn’t doing any favors by raising rates to fight inflation.


## Bitcoin Is the Exception as Stocks and Gold Struggle


Against that backdrop, bitcoin is up 29.8% since Aug 18, the only asset in our group with a double-digit gain. Bitcoin is not immune to macro, and it slipped about 3% between the September 9 buyback announcement and the September 11 close as yields rose. Even so, we think its performance is instructive on two fronts. Bitcoin is being driven mostly by idiosyncratic factors, and negative sentiment appears to be washed out.


The reaction to CLARITY is the best evidence for the second point. CLARITY, the industry's biggest legislative effort and years in the making, failed its vote on Sep 15. Bitcoin went from about $76.3k just before the vote to about $75.7k the next morning, a decline of less than 1% and hardly commensurate with the setback. It also didn’t react to the Fed's rate hike the following day as one might expect, rising roughly 1% over the 24 hours spanning the decision. A market that can absorb both a failed landmark bill and a rate hike without flinching is one where the sellers appear to be exhausted.


## The Break-Glass Bid Is Plausible, but Not Yet Proven


If bitcoin's floor was set by its own cycle, why has it kept rising as the US loses its grip on yields? One possibility is that investors are increasingly reaching for an asset that sits outside the system entirely. Bitcoin and digital assets function something like a supranational currency, one that no Treasury buyback or FOMC decision can reprice. If confidence in the government's ability to manage its own curve is eroding, we think it is reasonable that some capital is breaking glass and hitting the emergency button.


There are reasons to hold this loosely, though they also point to something more interesting. Bitcoin's first leg up came after the August 19 Treasury announcement, when yields dipped and it rallied alongside gold. That was not how bitcoin had been behaving, since for much of the past few years it has traded as a risk-on asset closely tied to equities. The better test came later. Since the September 21 local peak in bitcoin price, the 10Y has risen about 32 bps, from 4.95% to 5.27%, and bitcoin has given back only about 4%, a muted response for an asset that would typically be sold in a yield spike. One episode does not make a regime, but our interpretation is that this is early evidence bitcoin is starting to trade as a hedge against the fiat system rather than an S&P 500 beta play.


As long as Washington does not address the root of the rise in yields, a debt burden that crossed $40 trillion last month and a deficit that keeps adding to it, bitcoin and other digital assets will likely keep drawing flows from investors looking to step outside the fiat system.


## Agencies Push Ahead Post CLARITY; IRS Moves to Clamp Down on Tax Strategies


Agencies have made numerous actions after Congress failed to advance CLARITY and provide legislative clarity to the industry. Here's a summary of what each agency has done.


## SEC: Carves Narrow Path for Tokenized Stocks, Lowers Risks for Securities Classification


### Tokenized Stocks and AMMs.


We wrote about this[previously](https://www.bitgo.com/resources/blog/agencies-step-up-after-congress-fails-to-act/) , but just a quick summary, the SEC issued an order exempting Tokenized Securities Venues (TSVs) from the definition of "exchange," and certain liquidity providers from the definition of "dealer," for permissioned trading of tokenized NMS stocks through automated market makers (AMMs). The relief expires five years after publication and comes with numerous conditions which may limit their ultimate appeal.


### Securities Threshold Raised.


SEC staff also published FAQs that made it harder for a token to satisfy the "efforts of others" prong of the Howey test, and therefore harder for it to be sold as a security. In FAQs published September 25 and updated September 28, staff said that once a network is functional, work to maintain, improve or grow it is not an "essential managerial effort." Promises to keep doing that work therefore can't meet the prong. If the network also has no central party, issuer statements and buybacks are unlikely to create a new investment contract, a qualifier added September 28 that shows how much work a few words can do. We think this lowers securities-law risk for mature, decentralized networks, while early-stage tokens with an active issuer remain exposed.


## CFTC: Passive Software Gets a Pass, Tokenized Investments Approved


Passive Software. Also written about previously, the CFTC extended no-action relief granted to Phantom to all "Passive Software Providers." They will not face enforcement for failing to register as introducing brokers so long as they route user orders directly to registered exchanges, FCMs or IBs and never touch user assets or discretion over routing.


Tokenized Investments. FCMs and DCOs may invest customer funds in tokenized versions of permitted investments. The Divisions' September 24 FAQ update says this is allowed if the underlying asset is already a permitted investment, the token carries the same or functionally equivalent legal and economic rights, and the investment meets limits on liquidity, concentration and maturity. The tokens must also sit with an acceptable depository institution, and lets FCMs accept non-security crypto as margin, with capital charges of 2% on payment stablecoins and 20% on bitcoin and ether that deliberately mirror the SEC's broker-dealer treatment.


## IRS: Shuts Down 351 Conversions and Puts Crypto ETF Tax Strategies on Notice


The IRS released[Notice 2026-62](https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-drop/n-26-62.pdf) alongside[Rev. Rul. 2026-20](https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-drop/rr-26-20.pdf) , and the pairing has produced more confusion than clarity. The ruling addresses the "351 conversion," in which an investor contributes appreciated securities to a newly formed ETF structured as a regulated investment company (RIC), the corporate structure used by traditional mutual funds. Under the same plan, the ETF redeems an authorized participant using those securities, leaving the investor in a materially different portfolio with no recognized gain. The IRS treats the ETF as a conduit and the investor as having made a taxable exchange.


For crypto, the relevant piece is one section of the notice, since the ruling never mentions bitcoin. The notice flags RIC ETFs that hold digital assets directly or through grantor trusts and use in-kind redemptions to avoid recognizing gain that would count against the RIC income test. Treasury signals skepticism but stops short of a ban. Most U.S. spot crypto ETFs are grantor trusts rather than RICs, and 351 applies only to transfers to a corporation (RIC), so it was never a route into them. Neither document, however, addresses how an in-kind contribution of appreciated bitcoin to a grantor trust ETF is taxed, but we would not imply silence as approval.


Comments are due October 28, 2026, and future guidance could apply retroactively. We think anyone weighing a tax-deferred route into a bitcoin ETF should get a tax opinion on their specific structure.


## Friendly Agencies, But Written Law Would Provide more Durability


The direction of travel is clear, and it is encouraging. However, this is not yet as permanent as CLARITY would have been, despite what might be portrayed on social media. Staff FAQs and no-action letters carry no legal force by their own terms, and since Loper Bright ended Chevron deference, courts no longer defer to agencies on what a statute means. We think the best way to see this period is as a proving ground, where every compliant venue and well-run program sets a precedent building towards durable law.


## Schrödinger's Wallet: The $388M Bitget Exploit Shows Exchanges Are Still Crypto's Weakest Link


It is 2026, and exchange hacks, the problem that has dogged crypto since its earliest days, remain unsolved. The recent $388M exploit of Bitget is the latest reminder, and the data say it is not an outlier. Of the $12.7B lost to crypto hacks since 2020, exchanges account for $4.0B, or roughly 32%, making them the largest category by a comfortable margin. Bridges are second at $2.8B, and together the two represent more than half of all losses. We think that is not a coincidence, since both concentrate large pools of assets behind signing infrastructure that someone has to operate, and both have repeatedly shown that operating it is harder than designing it. Exchanges are not the whole story. Lending, yield and vault protocols, and DEXs together account for another $4.01B, so smart contract risk is real. But the exchange category is the one where the failure mode is an operational choice rather than a code bug, which makes it the most fixable.


## The Keys Were Fine. The Infrastructure Wasn't.


What happened at Bitget is instructive precisely because of what did not happen. The attackers never stole private keys. Instead, they breached an internal backend microservice and spoofed transaction queue data, which convinced Bitget's automated risk engine to pass forged withdrawal payloads straight to the signing engine. The signing engine then did what it was built to do, blindly signing and broadcasting the transfers. The cryptography held up, but the pipeline feeding it did not, and that pipeline is where the real trust assumption lived. To see how a firm ends up here, it helps to look at wallet architecture. Hot wallets are online, fast, fully automated and heavily exposed by design. Cold wallets are air-gapped and offline, and they require out-of-band, multi-party human verification before anything moves. Then there is the warm wallet, the Schrödinger's cat of crypto security, marketed as both fast and safe until someone opens the box.


## Warm Wallets Are Hot Wallets with Better Marketing


In our view, the promise of hot-wallet speed with cold-wallet safety is misleading. Speed comes from automation and safety comes from human friction, so a design that leaves the signing engine tied to an automated backend pipeline has kept the attack surface and removed the checkpoint. If one compromised service can feed a signer forged instructions, the signer is only as trustworthy as the weakest system upstream of it. The tradeoff between operational efficiency and security is real, and exchanges face genuine pressure to process withdrawals quickly. But warm wallets mostly obscure which side of that tradeoff an operator has chosen, and Bitget's experience suggests customers and counterparties are often not told.


## "User Funds Are Safe" Is Not the Same as "The System Is Safe"


Bitget deserves credit for backstopping the loss. The full amount falls within the coverage of its User Protection Fund, which currently holds over $464 million, and that is the right outcome for customers and a meaningful improvement over earlier eras when exchange failures meant permanent losses. But "user funds are safe" answers a narrower question than the one institutions should be asking. A well-capitalized “insurance” fund tells us who absorbs the loss, and it tells us nothing about whether the architecture that allowed the loss has been fixed.


## Every Exploit Fuels Global Insecurity


The industry cannot treat this as another day, another hack. Dismissing these breaches minimizes what is at stake, because crypto's security flaws now reach well beyond the affected platform. According to[Chainalysis](https://www.chainalysis.com/blog/crypto-hacking-stolen-funds-2026/) , more than $6.8 billion in stolen digital assets has been linked to North Korea sponsored actors, funds that directly support its nuclear and ballistic missile programs. Every insecure architecture is therefore a potential source of financing for a geopolitical threat, which raises the cost of complacency for exchanges, regulators and allocators alike. For institutional investors, the practical implication is to diligence custody and signing architecture as carefully as reserves and insurance. Ask whether withdrawals require independent human verification, and whether a compromised internal service could authorize a transfer on its own. The industry needs to stop accepting insecure architectures, technologies and business processes. Until it does, the next headline is a matter of time.
